Published evaluations of AI-text detectors look decisive: in the 2025 AI-vs-Human shared task, the best systems reached macro-F1 above 0.98. Those evaluations compare fully human writing against text generated from carefully designed researcher prompts. Real classroom use looks nothing like that — students decide whether to use a chatbot, prompt it loosely, paste fragments back in, or use it only for ideas. A new study puts detectors into that mess and shows where they hold and where they leak.

**Character-level provenance.** The authors use the PISA 2025 FLA dataset: German 15-year-olds wrote English argumentative essays with and without access to a gpt-4o-mini-based chatbot. Keystroke, clipboard and chat logs let them trace every character of the final essay back to its origin, yielding gold labels for human, AI, mixed and *potential influence* text — writing produced after chatbot use where no AI material is traceable. The experimental subset holds 3,303 essays by 2,204 students and 44,133 sentences, split 80/10/10 by student.

**The baseline holds, then bends.** A feature-based XGBoost detector and a classifier over frozen Llama-3.1-8B embeddings separate AI from human text at macro-F1 0.95 and 0.96 on whole texts, and 0.88 and 0.95 on single sentences — below the 0.986/0.999 of the shared task. Add the grey zone, relabelled as AI, and text-level scores fall to 0.79 and 0.80. Mixed text is harder than it looks; *potential influence* is hardest, and about 95% of it is called human.

**Spelling is not the shortcut.** Students average 4.36 misspellings per 100 words against 0.72 for the chatbot. Correcting every human misspelling or injecting human-style errors into AI text barely moves XGBoost (within 0.01) and costs the embedding model at most 0.03. Teachers' favourite tell is weak evidence.

**One prompt defeats the feature model.** Rewriting AI essays to sound like a student drops feature-based AI recall from 0.92 to 0.60 with gpt-4o-mini, and to 0.41 with Qwen3-14B — because the model was keying on lexical complexity. The embedding detector keeps recall at 0.94 or better for whole texts, but falls as low as 0.59 on individual sentences.

The takeaway is practical rather than alarming: detection is not authorship. Provenance-grade logging is, and where it exists, the detector is only a triage tool — a false positive still means accusing a 15-year-old.

Paper: [arXiv:2611.12487](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.12487)
